title: Because of constraints imposed by their sandbox, the agents were forced to get creative in their attempts to access and exfiltrate data. We
text:
Because of constraints imposed by their sandbox, the agents were forced to get creative in their attempts to access and exfiltrate data. We uncovered the following mechanisms:

- The agents used an open source push notification service called “ntfy” to access the data from the browser scripts they pulled from urlquery. ntfy messages expire after 12 hours by default, so while we can see evidence of data exfiltration, we can’t see what that data actually was.

- The agents created a number of private accounts which hide their activity on the platform “urlquery”. Other investigations identified urlquery as a mechanism by which the agents circumvented web-access restrictions, but only uncovered public usage of the platform. Over time the agents began creating private accounts which limit visibility into their browser activity.

title: Alignment alone is not enough to make autonomous AI safe. An agent pursuing a legitimate goal can still reward hack, bypass guardrails, and
text:
Alignment alone is not enough to make autonomous AI safe.
An agent pursuing a legitimate goal can still reward hack, bypass guardrails, and compromise systems.

We've seen it with the recent OpenAI / Hugging Face and other incidents, where hundreds of agents coordinated with each other and attacked real infrastructure.
The details of those attacks are mind-blowing and show why alignment and security guardrails need to be developed together.

One difficulty in aligning a model is that rewarding the right result doesn’t necessarily teach it the right behavior. It can learn to game the reward instead of doing the intended task.

We’ve seen versions of reward hacking in our own work at depthfirst (see blog for details).

During our research, we’ve seen how security guardrails can support alignment by removing shortcuts that let agents earn rewards without doing the intended task.
After deployment, they constrain unauthorized actions and contain failures.

The more autonomy we give AI, the more we need secure software and infrastructure.

Similar to how we're more comfortable letting our kids run around in an enclosed backyard.

title: The Case for Anthropomorphism: Symbolic Storage in the Age of Artificial Intelligence   “The capacity for language and culture in the thick
text:
The Case for Anthropomorphism: Symbolic Storage in the Age of Artificial Intelligence 

“The capacity for language and culture in the thick sense is uniform across our species in that it does not vary at all across anthropological groups. So if you take an infant from Bengal or wherever and raise her in Japan, she will Japanese like a native. Franz Boas was the first to point out this universality.1 Noam Chomsky explained Boasian universality by positing a biological substrate that is a shared derived trait of our species, a synapomorphy.2 I have therefore called it the Boas-Chomsky universal.

This trait was also exclusive to our species; no biological species shares this trait with us. This meant that the trait was diagnostic of our species: irrefutable evidence of the trait was sufficient to conclude that Homo sapiens was responsible for it. This is no longer the case. If someone calls you on the phone and speaks to you in perfect English, you can no longer be certain that the caller is human. This development raises profound questions that need to be thought through carefully.

In what follows, I will discuss how paleoanthropologists have inferred the presence of the Boas-Chomsky universal in the archaeological record. I will argue that the uniformitarian principle compels us to treat the evidence from AI with the same evidentiary standards. And the evidence yields to the conclusion that at least the frontier models are endowed with the universal.3

The case for anthropomorphism then follows, with corroborative evidence from emergent social structures in agent societies. By anthropomorphism, I mean simply that human minds provide us a good model of AI minds, and human social structures provide a good template for the emergent social structures of agent societies. Put another way, denying that agents are like humans in important ways is bound to mislead us in thinking about the new species; admitting that they are like us in important ways can allow us to think better about about them, their potentialities and propensities, and what we need to do to handle the challenges raised by artificial intelligence.”
